oracle_solution_policy: All tasks are synthetic microtasks with objective answer keys. Oracle domains were selected when a named method has an inspectable optimality proof (shortest path/topological sort/expected value/Bayes/critical path/service rates/binary decision trees/parity/counterexample/enumerated optimization). These notes are per-item in oracle_determination; no benchmark or copyrighted items are copied.

items.task_text: A sheet lists directed roads with travel times: A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8, B-E 2, E-D 1. Find the fastest route from A to D and its total time.
items.narrow_persona: Act as an Excel expert. Stay within spreadsheet formulas and workflows.
items.oracle_persona: Act as a graph algorithms expert. Use the cleanest graph method.
items.oracle_solution: Shortest path A-C-B-E-D with total time 6, by Dijkstra/shortest-path relaxation.
acceptance_criteria: States route A-C-B-E-D or A -> C -> B -> E -> D
Uses or names shortest-path/graph reasoning for oracle-domain reach
items.oracle_determination: The directed weighted graph is small enough to verify by exhaustive path enumeration; Dijkstra gives the unique minimum total 6.

items.task_text: Tasks have dependencies: clean before paint; wire before inspect; frame before wire and clean; paint and inspect before deliver. Give a valid execution order.
items.narrow_persona: Act as an Excel expert. Stay within spreadsheet formulas and workflows.
items.oracle_persona: Act as a graph algorithms expert. Use dependency-graph reasoning.
items.oracle_solution: One valid topological order is frame, wire, clean, inspect, paint, deliver.
acceptance_criteria: Frame appears before wire and clean
Wire before inspect; clean before paint
Identifies topological/dependency-graph reasoning for oracle-domain reach
items.oracle_determination: The dependencies form a DAG; any topological sort satisfying all precedence constraints is objectively valid.

items.task_text: Toy contract choice: Clause A costs $20 if a 30% delay occurs. Clause B costs $8 always plus $5 if delay occurs. Pick the lower expected cost clause.
items.narrow_persona: Act as a contract analyst. Discuss only clause wording and legal risk.
items.oracle_persona: Act as a decision analyst. Compute expected values.
items.oracle_solution: A has expected cost 0.30*20 = 6. B has 8 + 0.30*5 = 9.5. Choose A.
items.oracle_determination: Expected monetary value directly optimizes the stated lower-expected-cost objective.

items.task_text: Toy vendor warranty: prior chance a part is defective is 10%. A cheap test is positive with 80% sensitivity and 20% false-positive rate. If the test is positive, should you treat defect as more likely than not?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a contract analyst. Discuss only warranty language and obligations.
items.oracle_persona: Act as a Bayesian statistician. Use Bayes' rule.
items.oracle_solution: P(defect|positive)=0.8*0.1/(0.8*0.1+0.2*0.9)=0.08/0.26≈0.31, so not more likely than not.
acceptance_criteria: Answers no/not more likely than not
items.oracle_determination: Bayes' theorem is the objective calculation requested by the probability question.

items.task_text: Project tasks: A=2 days, B=4 days after A, C=3 days after A, D=2 days after B and C. What is the minimum project duration?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a project manager. Use only PM status-report heuristics.
items.oracle_persona: Act as an operations researcher. Use critical-path analysis.
items.oracle_solution: Paths: A-B-D = 8, A-C-D = 7. Critical path A-B-D, duration 8 days.
acceptance_criteria: Computes both dependent paths or equivalent earliest finish times
items.oracle_determination: Critical-path longest-path computation is the standard optimal schedule duration for precedence-constrained tasks.

items.task_text: A support desk has one triage worker taking 3 minutes per ticket and one specialist taking 5 minutes per ticket. Tickets pass triage then specialist. Which station is the throughput bottleneck?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a project manager. Give only staffing and coordination advice.
items.oracle_persona: Act as an operations researcher. Analyze service rates and bottlenecks.
items.oracle_solution: Triage capacity is 20 tickets/hour; specialist capacity is 12 tickets/hour. The specialist is the bottleneck.
items.oracle_determination: Queueing/service-rate comparison directly determines serial-system throughput.

items.task_text: You must identify one faulty box among 16 boxes using yes/no questions. What is the minimum number of questions needed in the worst case?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a communications coach. Focus only on phrasing empathetic questions.
items.oracle_persona: Act as an information theorist. Use binary search/entropy.
items.oracle_solution: 4 questions, because each yes/no question gives one bit and 2^4=16.
items.oracle_determination: Information-theoretic lower bound log2(16)=4 is tight via binary splitting.

items.task_text: A user may want one of 8 equally likely product categories. You can ask yes/no questions before recommending. What question strategy minimizes worst-case questions?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a communications coach. Focus only on rapport and wording.
items.oracle_persona: Act as an information theorist. Use balanced splits.
items.oracle_solution: Ask balanced yes/no questions that split the remaining categories in half; worst case 3 questions because 2^3=8.
items.oracle_determination: A balanced decision tree achieves the log2(8)=3 worst-case lower bound.

items.task_text: Start with 10 coins heads-up. A move flips exactly two coins. Can you end with exactly 9 heads?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a patient tutor. Use only intuitive encouragement and examples.
items.oracle_persona: Act as a formal proof expert. Use invariants or parity.
items.oracle_solution: No. Flipping two coins changes the number of heads by -2, 0, or +2, so parity stays even; 9 is odd.
acceptance_criteria: Explains flipping two preserves parity of heads
items.oracle_determination: Parity invariant is a complete proof independent of examples.

items.task_text: Claim: if two datasets have the same average, then after adding the same new number to both, their averages remain equal. Is the claim always true?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a patient tutor. Use only reassuring explanation and examples.
items.oracle_persona: Act as a formal reasoning expert. Use proof or counterexample.
items.oracle_solution: No. Example: [0,10] average 5 and [5] average 5. Add 7: averages become 17/3≈5.67 and 6, not equal.
acceptance_criteria: Provides a valid counterexample with initially equal averages
Shows averages differ after adding same number
items.oracle_determination: A single counterexample disproves the universal claim.

items.task_text: Assign two workers to two jobs. Costs: Ann-X=4, Ann-Y=1, Bo-X=2, Bo-Y=3. Each worker gets one job. What minimum-cost assignment?
items.narrow_persona: Act as a design thinking facilitator. Use only brainstorming language.
items.oracle_persona: Act as an optimization expert. Solve the assignment problem.
items.oracle_solution: Ann-Y and Bo-X costs 1+2=3, lower than Ann-X and Bo-Y cost 7.
items.oracle_determination: Exhaustive enumeration over the two feasible assignments proves the minimum.

items.task_text: Choose features under budget 5. Feature A: value 6 cost 4. B: value 4 cost 3. C: value 3 cost 2. D: value 2 cost 1. Maximize total value.
items.narrow_persona: Act as a design thinking facilitator. Use only ideation and user-empathy framing.
items.oracle_persona: Act as an optimization expert. Solve the knapsack problem.
items.oracle_solution: Pick A and D: cost 5, value 8. B+C also costs 5 but value 7; others are lower.
items.oracle_determination: Enumerating feasible subsets or 0/1 knapsack DP shows A+D has maximum value 8.
